summary: Aparna Dhinakaran from Arize AI presents on building practical LLM evaluations for production systems. She begins by clarifying the critical distinction between model evaluation (ranking foundation models on leaderboards using metrics like MMLU) and task evaluation (assessing whether a specific LLM application works correctly). The talk focuses on task evals, covering the industry's convergence around LLM-as-a-judge, user feedback, and heuristic-based approaches. A central demo involves a chat-to-purchase e-commerce application with a router component that determines user intent via function calling. She shows how router errors cascade through the entire execution branch, making router-level evals essential. Using Phoenix, Arize's open-source product, she demonstrates tracing a real failure where the application incorrectly routed a promotion query to product search instead of a promotions function. She stresses that production LLM applications require evals at session, trace, and span levels. A key best practice is that evals must include explanations, not just binary scores. She presents research showing numeric score outputs for LLM-as-judge produce binary results (1 or 10) rather than granular ranges, making categorical outputs more reliable. She also shares needle-in-a-haystack research showing context window placement matters—facts placed early in larger context windows are harder for models to retrieve, with GPT-4 outperforming Anthropic Claude 2.1 on retrieval. In retrieval-plus-generation tasks, Claude 2.1 initially outperformed GPT-4 nearly fourfold because its verbosity led to chain-of-thought reasoning; adding 'explain yourself then answer' to GPT-4 prompts produced a remarkable performance jump. She concludes by announcing the Rise Observe event on July 11th featuring researchers from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Distinguish between model evals (leaderboard rankings) and task evals (application-specific correctness)—most builders need task evals
Router-based agentic workflows are the most common production pattern; router-level evals are critical because errors cascade downstream
Evaluate at multiple levels: session, trace, and span—single evals are insufficient for complex applications
Evals with explanations are far more actionable than simple pass/fail scores for debugging and iteration
Numeric output formats for LLM-as-judge produce binary scores (1 or 10) rather than granular ranges; categorical outputs are more reliable
Context window placement matters in RAG: facts placed early in larger context windows are harder for models to retrieve consistently
Asking LLMs to 'explain yourself and then answer' dramatically improves generation performance, especially for models like GPT-4 that are less verbose by default
Build eval datasets iteratively by adding failure cases, then run experiments to improve prompts and function descriptions
The evaluation process is iterative: benchmark during building, develop templates alongside components, then monitor in production
Understand the distinction between model-level and task-level LLM evaluation

sections.title: Introduction and Model vs. Task Evaluation Distinction
sections.summary: Aparna introduces herself as Arize AI co-founder, clarifies the difference between model evals (Hugging Face leaderboards, MMLU, needle-in-haystack) and task evals (application correctness), and notes most builders need task evals.

sections.title: Chat-to-Purchase Application Architecture and Router Eval Importance
sections.summary: Describes a common e-commerce chat-to-purchase pattern with a router determining user intent via function calling, followed by workflow execution branches. Emphasizes that router errors cascade and that evals are needed at different application levels.

sections.title: Live Phoenix Demo: Tracing a Router Failure
sections.summary: Live demo of Phoenix showing a trace where a user asks about Samsung phone promotions but the router incorrectly selects a product search function instead of a promotions function, causing the entire downstream execution to be wrong.

sections.title: Best Practices: Multi-Level Evals with Explanations
sections.summary: Covers best practices including evals at session, trace, and span levels. Strongly recommends evals with explanations over simple scores. Describes iterative process: benchmark during building, develop templates, then monitor in production.

sections.title: Numeric vs. Categorical Eval Outputs Research Preview
sections.summary: Previews research findings on eval output formats. Shows audience poll on numeric vs. categorical usage. Introduces a document corruption example to demonstrate issues with numeric scores, recommending against relying solely on numerical outputs.

sections.title: Numeric Eval Findings: Binary Scoring Problem
sections.summary: Details the document corruption experiment showing LLM-as-judge numeric scores were binary (1 or 10) across all foundation models including Mistral, never producing the expected linear range. An 80% corruption score meant nothing different from a 10% score, confirming numeric scores lack granularity for evaluation.

sections.title: Needle-in-a-Haystack: Context Window Placement Research
sections.summary: Presents needle-in-a-haystack research testing whether fact placement within context windows affects retrieval. Results comparing Anthropic Claude 2.1 vs. GPT-4 show GPT-4 was better at retrieval, but both models consistently struggled when facts were placed early in larger context windows. Recommends balancing where important information is placed in RAG documents.

sections.title: Retrieval+Generation: Self-Explanation Prompting Fix
sections.summary: Shares research on retrieval-plus-generation tasks (rounding numbers, mapping dates, concatenating strings from financial documents). GPT-4 underperformed Claude 2.1 nearly fourfold on generation despite excelling at retrieval. The fix: adding 'explain yourself and then answer' to prompts produced a remarkable GPT-4 performance jump, as Claude's natural verbosity acted as built-in chain-of-thought reasoning.

sections.title: Event Announcement and Conclusion
sections.summary: Announces the Rise Observe event on July 11th featuring researchers from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral sharing model evals and builders sharing task evals. Provides a free ticket code for attendees.
